questions.prompt: Which pattern gives you readable test data like `aUser().withRole('admin').build()` while defaulting everything else?
questions.explanation: A Builder sets sensible defaults and lets each test override only what matters. Singleton restricts instances, Observer is about event notification and Adapter converts one interface to another.

questions.prompt: A Facade in a test framework can hide several page objects behind one business-level method such as `checkout.placeOrder(cart)`.
questions.explanation: That is exactly the Facade pattern: a simple interface over a more complex subsystem, so tests read as business flows.

questions.prompt: What problem does the Strategy pattern solve in a test framework?
options: Swapping interchangeable behaviours, such as different login methods (UI form, API token, SSO), behind one interface
questions.explanation: Strategy encapsulates a family of algorithms so the caller can choose one at runtime. It is not about instance count (Singleton) or cross-cutting logging (Decorator or listeners).

build() is called on a fresh builder each time. The first builder's withRole('admin') does not affect the second, so u2 has the default role 'user' and active true. Builders that return new objects avoid shared-state leaks between tests.

questions.prompt: Tests run in parallel share this driver holder and interfere with each other. What is the root cause?
options: A single static driver instance is shared across threads; it should be per thread (for example ThreadLocal) or injected per test
questions.explanation: A classic Singleton gives every thread the same browser session, so parallel tests click in each other's browser. Per-thread storage or dependency injection keeps sessions isolated.

questions.prompt: Which are signs a pattern is adding cost without value in your framework? Select all that apply.
options: A Factory with only one product and no plan for another
Three layers of abstraction to click one button
A Builder that lets each test set only the fields it cares about
New team members cannot find where a click actually happens
questions.explanation: Patterns should remove duplication or isolate change. Single-product factories, deep indirection and code nobody can trace are overhead. A Builder that cuts test data noise is earning its keep.

questions.prompt: In the Screenplay pattern, which element represents 'what the user wants to achieve', for example `PlaceOrder`?
questions.explanation: Actors have Abilities (such as BrowseTheWeb), perform Tasks (business goals made of Interactions) and ask Questions to check state. PlaceOrder is a Task.

questions.prompt: Every test needs a logged-in user and setup takes 20 seconds through the UI. You want tests to pick 'UI login' for the login tests and 'API token injection' for everything else, without if/else in every test. Which design fits best?
options: A Singleton that logs in once for the whole suite
A LoginStrategy interface with UiLogin and ApiLogin implementations, chosen per test or via configuration
Copying the login code into each test class
questions.explanation: Strategy lets the login method vary independently of the tests. A shared single login couples tests together and breaks isolation; copy-paste multiplies maintenance; a Decorator adds behaviour around calls rather than choosing an algorithm.

questions.prompt: You want every WebDriver action logged with timing, without editing each page object. Which approach is cleanest?
options: Add log statements to every page object method
Wrap the driver in a Decorator (or use Selenium's event-firing/listener support) that logs around each call
Use a Builder for the driver
questions.explanation: A Decorator or listener adds cross-cutting behaviour in one place and leaves page objects unchanged. Editing every method duplicates code and is easy to forget; Singleton and Builder do not add behaviour around calls.

coding.title: Test data builder
coding.explanation: Returning `this` makes calls chain. build() copies the items array and each item so callers get independent objects; without the copy two orders built from one builder would share the same array, a subtle source of test pollution.
hints: Set the defaults in the constructor.
Each fluent method changes a field and ends with `return this;`.

tests.name: built objects are independent
tests.code: const b = new OrderBuilder().withItem('A1',1); const o1 = b.build(); o1.items.push({sku:'X',qty:9}); o1.items[0].qty = 50; const o2 = b.build(); assertEqual(o2.items, [{sku:'A1',qty:1}])

coding.title: Driver config factory
coding.prompt:
Write `driverConfig(env)` (a Factory) that returns a config object:

- `'local'` -> `{ browser: 'chrome', headless: false, remoteUrl: null }`
- `'ci'` -> `{ browser: 'chrome', headless: true, remoteUrl: null }`
- `'grid'` -> `{ browser: 'firefox', headless: true, remoteUrl: 'http://grid:4444' }`

Any other value must throw an `Error` whose message contains `unknown environment`. Each call returns a fresh object.
coding.explanation: The factory centralises the decision of which browser setup to create, so tests just ask for an environment. Failing loudly on an unknown name stops a typo like 'cl' silently running against the wrong setup. The own-property check also rejects names such as 'toString'.
hints: A lookup object keyed by environment keeps this short.
Throw `new Error('unknown environment')` when the key is missing.
Use Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call so inherited names like 'toString' are rejected, and return a spread copy.

tests.name: unknown env throws
tests.code: let msg = ''; try { driverConfig('staging'); } catch (e) { msg = e.message; } assert(msg.includes('unknown environment'), 'expected an unknown environment error'); let m2=''; try { driverConfig('toString'); } catch (e) { m2 = e.message; } assert(m2.includes('unknown environment'), 'toString must be rejected')

tests.name: fresh object each call
tests.code: const a = driverConfig('ci'); a.headless = false; assertEqual(driverConfig('ci').headless, true)
